name: Wallets / ENS / on-chain identity
originator: Wallets: MetaMask (ConsenSys, 2016), Rainbow (2021), Phantom (2021), among many others. ENS: Nick Johnson / True Names Ltd / Ethereum Foundation grant (2017). On-chain identity broader ecosystem: Ethereum Attestation Service (EAS), Gitcoin Passport, Lens Protocol, Farcaster.
geography: Global. ENS: True Names Ltd registered in Singapore. MetaMask: ConsenSys (US/Global). Wallet usage concentrated in US, EU, East Asia, and emerging crypto markets in Southeast Asia, Latin America, and Africa. ENS domain registration skews toward English-speaking and crypto-native communities.
core_claim: Crypto wallets are self-sovereign identity instruments: you own your keys, you own your identity, no corporation can deplatform you. ENS extends this by providing human-readable names (artist.eth) for wallet addresses, creating a portable identity layer across the decentralized web. The broader on-chain identity movement claims that verifiable credentials, attestations, and reputation accumulated on-chain can replace platform-dependent profiles, giving artists a persistent, cross-platform presence anchored to cryptographic proof rather than corporate permission.
medium_specificity: Directly enables digital art's identity layer. In traditional art, identity is mediated by galleries, institutions, and reputation networks. In digital art, the wallet IS the artist's identity -- it signs transactions, mints works, collects art, and accumulates on-chain history. ENS names become artist brands (XCOPY.eth, deafbeef.eth). This is specific to digitally native practice: the identity and the creative output share the same cryptographic substrate. The wallet is simultaneously tool, identity, portfolio, and provenance record.
relation_to_attention_economy: Complex dual role. ENS names and wallet identities enable artists to build presence outside attention-economy platforms (no algorithm between artist and collector). However, the social layer around wallets (tracking whale wallets, following .eth profiles on Twitter/X, Etherscan stalking) creates its own attention dynamics. The transparency of on-chain activity turns every transaction into potential social signal. Wallet-based identity can resist platform attention capture (portable, self-owned) but is frequently instrumentalized for attention purposes (displaying .eth name on Twitter for social capital).
relation_to_intention: Infrastructure-neutral tending toward intention. Wallets as self-sovereign identity tools serve declared structural needs: authentication, ownership, portability. ENS serves the structural need for human-readable addressing. However, the speculative dynamics around ENS domain trading (.eth squatting, three-digit name speculation) are pure attention/capture. The attestation and reputation layers (EAS, Gitcoin Passport) are more clearly intention-native, serving structural needs for trust and verification.
revenue_model: ENS: Annual domain registration fees ($5/year for 5+ character names, higher for shorter names) paid in ETH. ENS DAO treasury funded by registration revenue. MetaMask: Swap fees (0.875% on built-in token swaps), portfolio services. Other wallets: freemium models, transaction facilitation fees, institutional custody services. On-chain identity protocols: mostly grant-funded or token-subsidized. EAS: open-source, no direct revenue model.
market_position: Infrastructure layer. Wallets are the universal access point for all Web3 interactions. ENS is the dominant naming service on Ethereum. Together they form the identity substrate beneath all NFT platforms, DAOs, and DeFi. Not a marketplace but the prerequisite for marketplace participation.
price_range: ENS: $5/year for standard names. Premium/short names can cost thousands (three-letter .eth names have sold for $100K+). Wallet software: free. Hardware wallets (Ledger, Trezor): $70-250. No direct art pricing.
volume_trend_2024_2026: ENS registrations peaked in 2022 (2.2M+ new registrations) and declined significantly with the crypto downturn. Renewals remain steady for established names. MetaMask monthly active users peaked at 30M+ in 2022, declined to roughly 10-20M range. Wallet usage is recovering with broader crypto market recovery in 2024-2025. New entrants like Coinbase Wallet and embedded wallets (account abstraction via ERC-4337) are reshaping the landscape. The trend is toward wallet abstraction (invisible wallets embedded in apps) rather than standalone wallet products. [uncertain]
collector_demographics: Broad crypto-native base. Artist wallet users skew toward: crypto-native digital artists, generative artists, photographers entering Web3. Collector wallet users: crypto-wealthy individuals, speculative traders, institutional funds (via custodial wallets). ENS users: identity-conscious crypto participants, brands entering Web3. Geographic concentration in US, EU, East Asia. The unbanked and underbanked populations were a stated target but actual adoption among these groups remains limited.
sustainability: Wallets are sustainable as long as blockchain networks operate -- they are basic infrastructure with clear utility. ENS sustainability is strong: recurring registration fees, DAO treasury, and essential utility create a durable model independent of speculation. MetaMask's swap fee model faces competition from aggregators and embedded wallets. The broader identity ecosystem faces funding challenges: many projects are grant-dependent. Account abstraction (ERC-4337, EIP-7702) may make current wallet UX obsolete while strengthening the underlying identity model. Long-term sustainability is tied to blockchain adoption generally, not to art-specific dynamics. [uncertain]
toolchain: Wallets: MetaMask (browser extension, mobile), Rainbow, Phantom, Coinbase Wallet, Rabby, Frame. Hardware: Ledger, Trezor, GridPlus. ENS: ens.domains frontend, ENS SDK, ethers.js ENS resolution. Account abstraction: Safe (formerly Gnosis Safe), Pimlico, Alchemy Account Kit, Privy. Identity/attestation: Ethereum Attestation Service, Gitcoin Passport SDK, Lens Protocol SDK, Farcaster Hub. Developer integration: WalletConnect, wagmi, viem, RainbowKit.
relation_to_AI: Nascent but emerging. AI agents increasingly need wallet-based identity for autonomous on-chain transactions (purchasing compute, storing data, minting). The concept of 'AI wallets' or agent wallets is an active frontier. For artists, the question is: if an AI agent has a wallet and mints art, whose identity is it? Wallet-based identity assumes a human key-holder, which AI agents problematize. Some projects explore wallet-based authentication for proving human authorship (proof of humanity). This is becoming a critical intersection as AI-generated content floods digital art spaces.
liveness: Persistent identity layer. Wallets are always-on cryptographic identities. ENS names resolve in real-time. On-chain reputation accumulates continuously. Not static (identity evolves with transactions) but not performative in the artistic sense. The 'liveness' is in the ongoing accumulation of on-chain history rather than any real-time generative quality.
aesthetic_vocabulary: Underdeveloped for art purposes. Technical vocabulary is mature: 'self-custody,' 'seed phrase,' 'signing,' 'delegation,' 'attestation,' 'Soulbound tokens,' 'account abstraction,' 'ENS resolution.' Art-specific identity vocabulary is thin. There is no established critical language for how wallet identity shapes artistic practice, though practitioners have informal terms ('wallet stalking,' 'PFP identity,' 'on-chain presence,' 'degen culture'). The vocabulary for discussing how on-chain identity fragments or unifies artistic presence is almost entirely absent.
tendency_axis_position: Openness <-> Enclosure: Open at protocol level (ENS is open-source, wallets are interoperable). Enclosed at UX level (MetaMask's dominance creates de facto lock-in, seed phrase complexity excludes). | Commons <-> Capture: ENS DAO and open standards lean commons. MetaMask swap fees and proprietary wallet features lean capture. ENS domain speculation is pure capture. | Spectacle <-> Infrastructure: Pure infrastructure, though .eth names on Twitter/X profiles are spectacle-adjacent social signaling. | Individual <-> Collective: Strongly individual (self-sovereign identity is inherently individualistic). Multisig wallets and DAO identity provide some collective dimension.
openness: Mixed. ENS protocol is open-source and governed by a DAO. Most wallet protocols (WalletConnect) are open standards. MetaMask code is open-source under a modified license. However, the UX layer creates practical enclosure: MetaMask's market dominance, Infura dependency for default RPC endpoints, and the complexity of running your own node. Account abstraction standards (ERC-4337) are open. The identity layer is more open than traditional platform identity but less open than it appears due to infrastructure dependencies.
governance_model: ENS: DAO governance with ENS token holders voting on protocol changes, treasury allocation, and working group mandates. Constitution-based governance with delegate system. MetaMask: Corporate governance (ConsenSys). Hardware wallets: Corporate governance (Ledger SA, SatoshiLabs). EAS: Open-source project with community governance. The wallet ecosystem overall lacks unified governance -- each product is governed independently, and the identity standards emerge through Ethereum's EIP process (rough consensus and running code).
data_sovereignty: Strong in principle, weaker in practice. Self-custody wallets give users full control over their keys and identity. ENS names are owned by the registrant (NFT-based ownership). On-chain data is fully portable -- any wallet can read any address's history. However: seed phrase loss means permanent identity loss. MetaMask's default Infura RPC means ConsenSys can see all user requests. ENS metadata stored on centralized servers for avatar/profile features. Hardware wallet firmware is often proprietary. True sovereignty requires technical sophistication most users lack.
interoperability: High. Ethereum addresses are universal identifiers across all EVM-compatible chains. ENS names resolve across Ethereum L1, L2s (with CCIP-Read/EIP-3668), and increasingly on non-EVM chains. WalletConnect enables cross-wallet, cross-dApp connectivity. However: non-EVM chains (Solana, Tezos) have separate identity systems (.sol, .tez names). Cross-chain identity is fragmented. No universal identity standard spans all blockchain ecosystems. For A(DAI) graph-readiness: wallet addresses are natural node identifiers, and ENS provides human-readable labels, but the lack of cross-chain standards is a gap.
preservation_strategy: Identity preserved by blockchain permanence. Wallet addresses and transaction history are permanently recorded on-chain. ENS names require renewal (can lapse if not renewed). The identity itself is as permanent as the blockchain. However, the meaning of that identity (who the person is, what they intended, their artistic context) is not preserved -- only the bare transaction record. Profile metadata (avatar, bio, social links) stored off-chain is fragile.
consent_architecture: Wallet-based consent is binary but user-controlled: sign or don't sign. Every on-chain interaction requires explicit wallet signature (consent via cryptographic action). This is stronger than platform consent (no 'agree to terms' click-through without reading). However: transaction transparency means all activity is public by default (no consent for observation). Token airdrops arrive without consent. ENS names can be registered by others (someone can register yourname.eth before you). No granular consent for how on-chain identity data is used by third parties.
relation_to_traditional_art_world: Tension and slow integration. Traditional galleries and auction houses have begun accepting crypto payments and recognizing wallet-based collector identity. Christie's and Sotheby's integrated wallet connections for NFT sales. However, the traditional art world's identity system (gallery representation, CV, institutional affiliation) is fundamentally different from wallet-based identity. Artists face a split identity: their .eth name carries weight in Web3 but means nothing at a gallery dinner. Museums acquiring NFTs grapple with institutional wallet management and key custody. ENS identity does not map to traditional art-world reputation structures.
what_it_enables: Self-sovereign artist identity independent of any platform. Pseudonymous practice (create and sell art without revealing legal identity). Portable reputation: on-chain history follows the artist across platforms. Direct artist-collector relationships without intermediary platforms. Verifiable provenance through cryptographic signatures. Cross-platform identity coherence (same wallet on Art Blocks, fxhash, SuperRare, Foundation). Programmable identity through smart contract wallets (multisig for collectives, automated royalty splits).
what_it_lacks: Human-readable context for identity (a wallet address reveals transactions but not intentions, influences, or artistic statement). Recovery mechanisms that don't compromise self-sovereignty (seed phrase loss = identity loss). Cross-chain identity unification. Integration with traditional art world credentials. Privacy-preserving reputation (proving credentials without revealing all transaction history). Collective identity infrastructure beyond basic multisig. Meaningful reputation beyond 'what you bought and sold.' No mechanism for artistic lineage, mentorship, or community relationship mapping. Identity verification that balances pseudonymity with accountability.
who_is_excluded: Non-crypto-literate artists face steep onboarding barriers (seed phrases, gas fees, wallet security). Artists in jurisdictions where crypto is restricted or banned. Individuals without government ID (needed for fiat-to-crypto onramps). Those who cannot afford hardware wallets or gas fees. Artists who value privacy but cannot navigate the technical complexity of privacy-preserving tools. Older practitioners unfamiliar with digital infrastructure. Communities without reliable internet access. Artists who want to revise or retract their public identity (immutable on-chain history prevents this). Collectives and collaborative practices are poorly served by individual wallet identity models.
frontier_signal: Established infrastructure undergoing radical transformation. Wallets and ENS are established. The frontier is account abstraction (ERC-4337, EIP-7702), which eliminates seed phrases, enables social recovery, and allows gas sponsorship -- potentially removing the biggest barriers to adoption. Also frontier: AI agent wallets, decentralized identity standards (DID/Verifiable Credentials integration with wallets), and privacy-preserving identity (ZK proofs of reputation without revealing transaction history). Smart accounts that embed identity, permissions, and recovery into a single programmable entity.
discovery_mechanism: Word of mouth in crypto communities. Platform onboarding flows (OpenSea, Art Blocks prompt wallet connection). Developer documentation and tutorials. ENS marketing and social media presence. Twitter/X .eth profile culture. Wallet provider marketing. Not discovered through traditional art channels.
attention_dependency: Low for core infrastructure function. Wallets work regardless of social media. ENS resolution works regardless of attention. However, the social signaling layer (.eth names on Twitter, wallet-watching culture) is highly attention-dependent. The speculative ENS domain market is attention-driven. Core identity function: attention-independent. Social/reputational layer: moderately attention-dependent.
intention_alignment: Infrastructure-native with mixed signals. Self-sovereign identity serves declared structural needs of artists (ownership, portability, authentication). ENS naming serves structural needs (human-readable addressing). However, ENS domain speculation, wallet-watching culture, and the social signaling of .eth names serve attention capture rather than structural needs. The infrastructure leans intention-native; the culture built around it often leans attention-native.
commons_contribution: Moderate commons contribution. ENS is a public naming system governed by a DAO -- genuinely commons-oriented. Open wallet standards (WalletConnect, EIP-4337) are commons infrastructure. On-chain transaction data is publicly readable (radical transparency as commons). However, identity data is raw and unstructured -- it contributes data but not knowledge to the commons. No shared vocabulary or structured intelligence emerges from wallet data without additional interpretive infrastructure (which is what A(DAI) aims to provide).
provenance_type: Ownership provenance primarily. Wallet-based identity tracks: who minted, who bought, who sold, who holds. This is strong ownership provenance but almost zero meaning provenance. The wallet does not record why an artwork was created, what it means, how it was received, or how its interpretation evolved. ENS adds a thin identity layer (name, avatar) but no interpretive context. The provenance is financial and transactional, not cultural or critical.
temporal_logic: Archival and accumulative. On-chain identity is a permanent, growing record of all transactions. The temporal logic is linear accumulation -- each transaction adds to the history. No cyclical, tidal, or anticipatory dynamics. ENS names have expiration dates, adding a renewal temporal logic. Account abstraction may introduce new temporal dynamics (programmable identity that evolves based on rules rather than just transaction history).
absence_handling: Does not address absence meaningfully. Wallet identity records what happened on-chain but has no mechanism for representing what didn't happen, who isn't present, or what is missing. Empty wallets are invisible. Artists who leave the space simply stop transacting -- there is no 'departure' record. The absence of women, non-Western artists, and non-crypto-native practitioners from on-chain identity systems is a massive structural gap that the infrastructure itself cannot surface.
coherence_vs_consensus: Technical consensus (network agrees on transaction validity) but no cultural coherence. Wallet identity is a bare fact layer -- it records what happened without interpretation. There is no mechanism for multiple valid readings of an identity (the transaction history is the transaction history). This is neither coherence nor consensus in the cultural sense -- it is simply data without interpretation.
contestability: Low contestability of on-chain record (transactions are immutable). High contestability of ENS governance (DAO voting, delegate debates). Moderate contestability of identity interpretation (anyone can present their own reading of a wallet's history). The identity itself is uncontestable (cryptographic proof), but its meaning is entirely open to interpretation.
forkability: Partially forkable. The protocols are open-source and can be forked. However, the critical value -- the accumulated identity (transaction history, ENS name recognition, reputation) -- cannot be forked. You can fork ENS code but not the .eth namespace. You can fork MetaMask but not users' seed phrases. Identity network effects create strong barriers to practical forking.
what_adai_should_adopt: Wallet addresses as stable node identifiers in the knowledge graph -- every practitioner node can link to verifiable on-chain identity. ENS-style human-readable naming for graph entities. The self-sovereign principle: artist identity in A(DAI) should be artist-controlled, not platform-assigned. Cryptographic signing as consent mechanism (artists sign to opt in to knowledge graph inclusion). The portability principle: identity data in A(DAI) should be exportable and usable elsewhere. Study account abstraction patterns for flexible, recoverable identity design.
what_adai_should_refuse: The reductive identity model: a wallet is not an artist. A(DAI) must build identity that includes intention, context, relationships, and meaning -- not just transaction history. The radical transparency default (all activity public) -- A(DAI) needs privacy-respecting identity. The individual-first identity model that poorly serves collectives, scenes, and collaborative practices. ENS-style domain speculation dynamics. The technical barrier that excludes non-crypto-literate participants. The absence of departure/absence/exclusion tracking.
structural_tension: Wallet-based identity provides a uniquely strong foundation -- cryptographic, self-sovereign, cross-platform -- but it captures only the thinnest slice of artistic identity. A(DAI) needs the cryptographic trust layer without the reductionism. The tension: how to build rich, contextual, meaning-laden artist identity (which requires subjective, interpretive data) atop a substrate designed for objective, transactional data. A(DAI) must bridge the gap between 'what you did on-chain' and 'who you are as a practitioner' -- this is the identity problem the field has not solved.
regulatory_exposure: Growing regulatory pressure. KYC/AML requirements increasingly applied to wallet onramps (exchanges, fiat gateways). Travel Rule (FATF) requires identity disclosure for transactions above thresholds. EU MiCA regulation imposes requirements on crypto service providers including wallet providers. ENS names create pseudonymity concerns for regulators. Self-custody wallets remain largely unregulated but face potential restrictions. US infrastructure broker rules could impact wallet providers. The tension between self-sovereign identity and regulatory identity requirements is unresolved and intensifying. [uncertain]
ip_model: ENS names are owned as NFTs (ERC-721) -- registrants have property rights. Wallet software is variously licensed (MetaMask: modified ConsenSys license; many wallets are open-source). On-chain identity data is public by default -- no IP protection for transaction history. Artists' on-chain activity is observable by anyone. No DRM or access control for identity data.
opt_in_vs_opt_out: Opt-in for wallet creation and ENS registration (active choice). However, observation of on-chain activity is opt-out impossible (anyone can watch any address). Token airdrops and spam NFTs arrive without consent (forced opt-in). ENS name registration by others of your name/brand is possible without consent. The consent model is strong for actions you take but absent for actions others take involving your address.
platform_dependency: Moderate. Wallets depend on RPC providers (Infura, Alchemy) for blockchain access -- significant centralization risk. MetaMask defaults to Infura (ConsenSys-owned). ENS depends on Ethereum L1 (highly decentralized). Hardware wallets depend on manufacturer firmware updates. WalletConnect depends on relay servers. The dependency is distributed across multiple providers but the default configurations concentrate risk. Running your own Ethereum node eliminates most dependencies but requires technical expertise.
network_effects: Very strong. Wallets benefit from universal adoption: every dApp needs wallet connection, every user needs a wallet. ENS benefits from social adoption: .eth names gain value as more people recognize and use them. MetaMask's market dominance creates lock-in effects. The identity layer has winner-take-most dynamics tempered by open standards (any wallet can replace MetaMask for core functions). ENS's first-mover advantage in naming is extremely strong -- competing naming services (.sol, Unstoppable Domains) fragment rather than displace.
post_crash_trajectory: Stable and evolving. Wallet infrastructure is essential regardless of market conditions -- even in bear markets, users need wallets. MetaMask active users declined from peak but recovered with 2024-2025 crypto market uptick. ENS registrations declined but renewals held steady, indicating retained utility. The major shift is toward account abstraction: embedded wallets, social login, passkey-based authentication -- moving from 'every user manages a seed phrase' to 'wallet invisible in app experience.' This is a fundamental UX transformation that could dramatically expand access. The post-crash trajectory is less about recovery and more about metamorphosis of the wallet concept itself. [uncertain]
